title: Why Texas Is Making Data Centers Wait | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z's Ryan McEntush explains why Texas froze new data-centre permits (474 GW queue, speculative filings, community distrust) and lays out how interconnection, behind-the-meter power, flexibility and equipment constraints shape the path to hundreds of gigawatts.

insights.claim: ERCOT's large-load queue grew from 63 GW at end-2024 to 474 GW by June 2026, more than five times record peak demand and about 90% data centers, prompting Texas to escalate from requiring data centers to pay for upgrades to a freeze on all new permits.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: The Texas pause delays data-centre energization and shifts developers toward other regions and on-site power.

insights.claim: Developers spam speculative projects across multiple sites, often with no customer and no experience, so planners cannot tell which are real and do not want ratepayers funding upgrades for projects that never arrive.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Expect tighter deposits and screening that favor credible, funded developers.

insights.claim: Community trust is a second driver: only 28 of 377 companies had answered a state survey on resource use as of June, and Hood County commissioners were asked to approve a tax waiver for 'Project Patriot' without knowing the company, with 56% of Texas voters in an August poll saying more data centers would hurt local bills.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Social license is now a binding constraint on data-centre siting.

insights.claim: The pause is harder to defend for developers that have funded their first phase or use emergency-only generators, and the author argues Texas should narrow it, with an October 19 update to the governor the obvious starting point.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Watch the October 19 update for a narrowing of the freeze.

insights.claim: Large loads used to buy power on paper through financial contracts, but the grid is now stretched so nearly any new large load needs upgrades, and fully connecting a large data center can take 5 to 10 years.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Time to power, not electricity price, is the key competitive variable.
insights.locator: What connecting to the grid actually means

insights.claim: ERCOT's Batch Zero studies large loads of 75 MW or more together, but ERCOT has paused approvals to switch on, including 17 projects that finished all other steps, until an audit's December report settles eligibility.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Texas data-centre timelines and load forecast are on hold until December.
insights.locator: What connecting to the grid actually means

insights.claim: New PUCT large-load rules effective October 8 charge a flat $100,000 study fee plus a $50,000 per MW deposit, but a failing project forfeits only 20% of the deposit, a thin filter against speculation.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Speculative queue clogging may persist despite the new rules.
insights.locator: What connecting to the grid actually means

insights.claim: ERCOT can lose only about 3.2 GW of load at once before causing issues, so a new voltage ride-through rule requires data centers to stay connected through routine faults.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Data-centre load behavior is now a grid reliability issue.
insights.locator: What connecting to the grid actually means

insights.claim: Regulators in July proposed charging large loads on all 12 monthly peaks instead of summer peaks so they pay in proportion to the size of their electricity pipes.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Raises transmission cost for large loads that currently skip peak-hour demand.
insights.locator: What connecting to the grid actually means

insights.claim: Colocation beside existing plants faces regulatory pushback: FERC rejected Talen's bid to send Amazon's Susquehanna campus more power directly, and Texas approvals of CyrusOne's 760 MW Freestone campus and Crusoe's Armstrong County sites require cutting load within 30 minutes or shedding entire load.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Co-located power deals carry curtailment obligations and cost-shifting scrutiny.
insights.locator: What connecting to the grid actually means

insights.claim: Idle GPUs cost far more than the electricity to run them, so developers pursue time to power with on-site generation, but nearly every site plans to connect to the grid as soon as possible because on-site power almost always costs more.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: On-site power is a bridge, not an end state; grid connection remains the endgame.
insights.locator: What bringing your own power solves

insights.claim: SemiAnalysis tracks 75 GW of equipment orders for behind-the-meter assets, much of which may be 'ghost capacity' missing from EIA grid-connected surveys.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Demand for gas engines, turbines, and batteries is larger than grid statistics suggest.
insights.locator: What bringing your own power solves / Getting to hundreds of gigawatts

insights.claim: Islanded sites face reliability problems: gas plants can fail together as in Winter Storm Uri, a 1 GW campus needs 14 GWh of batteries for one 14-hour winter night (about half of ERCOT's batteries as of June), and some buyers accept 99% uptime, about 88 hours of downtime a year.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Buyers trade reliability for speed, favoring modular gas engines and batteries.
insights.locator: What bringing your own power solves

insights.claim: AI workload swings at xAI's Memphis site of 10 to 20 MW several times a second wore out turbine shafts until xAI added 150 MW of Tesla Megapacks, so expect more batteries as rack power density grows.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Energy storage is a growing complement to on-site generation for AI campuses.
insights.locator: What bringing your own power solves

insights.claim: Duke researchers estimate ERCOT could add about 10 GW of new load without new generation if that load gave up 0.5% of its yearly grid electricity, and a PJM study found 20% flexibility per GW of data centre saves other customers $78 million a year.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Flexible load is a faster route to interconnection.

insights.claim: Batch Zero offers two flexible paths, bring your own power with one-minute cutback (11 projects chose it) or agree to automatic cuts, but it still plans upgrades for full campus load so flexibility speeds connection without shrinking upgrades.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Planners could size upgrades smaller by crediting flexibility and distributed resources.

insights.claim: Distributed resources can substitute for grid upgrades: about 80 MW of strategically sited home batteries could resolve all overloads from a hypothetical 100 MW Fort Worth data centre, per a Piq Energy study using Base Power data.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Aggregated batteries and grid-enhancing hardware are investable alternatives to wires.

insights.claim: Running 100 GW all year is 876 TWh, about a fifth of US 2025 consumption, while planned 2026 solar, wind and gas additions would produce only about 150 TWh, a sixth of that.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Gap between AI power ambitions and the planned supply pipeline is large.

insights.claim: Gas is popular because it runs when needed, but running 100 GW at gas rates would be nearly 8% of US energy-related emissions, and equipment availability, not fuel, is the constraint, pushing buyers to reciprocating engines and fuel cells.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Gas equipment makers are bottlenecks; alternatives gain share.

insights.claim: China makes more than 80% of the world's solar components and battery cells, creating supply-chain and policy risk for US solar scaling despite Elon Musk's goal of 200 GW a year of US solar manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: US solar and battery buildout depends on Chinese supply and trade policy.

insights.claim: Large power transformers take more than two years to arrive, and the FCC and an August emergency order may bar Chinese-made grid equipment, so transformers, switchgear, crews and 765 kV lines gate all power sources.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Grid equipment is a durable bottleneck across all power sources.

insights.claim: Startups can break into the power equipment market through integration or business model like Base Power, or through better technology like Heron Power, but incumbents remember the $22bn GE Power write-down from the last turbine boom and new vendors face a cold-start problem.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Shortage-driven 'worse but faster' pitches may not survive when supply catches up.

insights.claim: Past 2030 power ownership may consolidate under vertically integrated tech companies like Google (via its purchase of Intersect) or oil and gas firms and neo-utilities such as Chevron, Williams, NRG and NextEra building private grids, if law allows.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Watch for utility structures that allow multi-customer private grids; Utah's SB 132 is an early example.

insights.claim: Analyst Hans Royal estimates inference could pay $5,600 per MWh for power and still earn a decent return, nearly 60 times what the average US industrial customer pays.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: AI buyers can fund grid upgrades others cannot, which also strains local prices.

insights.claim: Berkeley Lab found states with the most load growth from 2019 to 2025 generally saw average prices fall after inflation, but in PJM the market monitor says data centers account for 38% of the latest capacity bill, about $6.3 billion.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Whether load growth cuts or raises rates depends on who pays fixed costs.

insights.claim: Google's $443 million upfront payment toward an Entergy solar plant in Arkansas is counted as prepayment so Entergy can still seek full cost plus return from all customers, an example of why fine print matters.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Community-benefit deals can still shift costs to ratepayers.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers covering a town's power bills could pencil: covering about 17,000 meters at Oregon's Umatilla Electric would cost about $30 million a year, under 0.5% of what a 1 GW campus costs to own and run.
insights.speaker: Ryan McEntush
insights.so_what: Ratepayer-protection and community-benefit packages are likely to become standard.
